short: Cheap, abundant iron democratises tools and weapons after the Bronze Age collapse.
full:
Iron is a poorer metal than bronze in some respects, and much harder to work — it requires far higher temperatures and skilled carburisation to make usable steel. Its advantage is abundance. Iron ore is found almost everywhere, so once the technique spread, tools and weapons no longer depended on fragile international tin routes.

The Iron Age follows the Bronze Age collapse from around 1200 BCE. Its social consequences were profound: iron ploughshares opened heavier soils to agriculture, and iron weapons could arm far larger forces than palace-controlled bronze ever had. In the Near East and Mediterranean the period shades into Classical Antiquity from roughly 550 BCE, though the two overlap considerably.
